title: Cache Invalidation Strategies
description: Learn when and how to remove or refresh stale cached data to keep systems consistent and reliable.

data.text: Cache invalidation is the process of removing or marking cached data as stale when the underlying source data changes. It is one of the hardest problems in computer science because there is no universal solution: the right strategy depends on the consistency requirements, write frequency, and latency tolerance of your system.

A cache without invalidation will eventually serve outdated data. In user-facing systems, stale data can show incorrect prices, missing comments, or old inventory counts. In backend systems, stale metadata can cause incorrect routing, duplicated processing, or security issues. Good invalidation keeps caches useful without turning them into a liability.

data.caption: Common cache invalidation approaches
data.definition:
graph TD
    W[Write to Source] --> I{Invalidate?}
    I -->|Yes| P[Purge / Delete Cache Entry]
    I -->|No| T[Wait for TTL Expiry]
    P --> N[Next Read Fetches Fresh Data]
    T --> N

data.title: Popular Invalidation Approaches:
items: TTL-based expiration: The cache automatically removes entries after a fixed duration. Simple and widely applicable, but may allow stale data between writes and expiry.
Write-through invalidation: Every write updates the source and immediately invalidates or updates the corresponding cache entry. Strongly consistent, but adds write latency.
Event-driven invalidation: A message or event notifies caches to invalidate entries when data changes. Scalable and decoupled, but requires reliable event delivery.

Versioned cache keys: Instead of invalidating old entries, writes change the cache key so old entries become unreachable. Eliminates explicit deletion but can increase memory usage until old entries expire.

data.title: Practical Tip
data.text: Combine TTL with targeted invalidation. A short TTL bounds staleness automatically, while event-driven invalidation keeps hot data fresh without waiting for expiry.

In system design interviews, you should explicitly discuss cache invalidation when you propose caching. Interviewers often probe whether you considered data consistency. Mention the trade-offs between freshness, write latency, and operational complexity. If you are unsure about write frequency, default to TTL with short durations and explain that you would tighten invalidation once real traffic patterns are known.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Invalidation prevents caches from serving stale data
TTL expiration is simple but allows bounded staleness
Write-through and event-driven approaches reduce staleness at the cost of complexity
Always discuss invalidation when proposing caching in interviews
data.takeaway: The best invalidation strategy balances freshness requirements against write overhead and operational complexity.
